Rule 14.115 and S12

S12, the shift arrows map at a desk Reply 1 You decide

Board 1 approved S12 drawn 1,024 px wide. The guide’s column is narrower than that at every desk width, so the approved drawing now sits in a frame 1,024 px wide that scrolls sideways, widened over the chapter list from a 1,280 px window. The other choice is a stacked tile: each state’s code over its figure, with the arrow beneath, which fits a drawing 618 px wide or more, the guide’s column from a 1,104 px window.

Recommended Take the stacked tile. It keeps board 1’s arrows, figures, scale rule, inks and words, and a reader at a 1,440 px window sees the whole map in the column with the chapter list in place. Where the column is narrower than 618 px, from a 1,024 to a 1,103 px window, hold the stacked tile in a frame 618 px wide that scrolls 62 px, in place of the 468 px the 1,024 px frame scrolls there. The cost is shorter arrows and a change to a drawing you approved; the engineer measures the kit’s bytes before it is built.

What changed
As built, at a 1,440 px window the frame shows 943 of the drawing’s 1,024 px, from Alaska to New Jersey and Connecticut; Maine, New Hampshire and Rhode Island sit past its edge until an 81 px scroll, and a line above the map says so. At a 1,024 px window the column is 558 px wide; inside its edges the frame shows 556 px of the drawing and scrolls the other 468. While S12 is in view the chapter list on the left is hidden. The stacked tile at a 1,440 px window draws the whole map in the column, 723 px wide, in tiles 54 px wide, with every code, figure and arrow inside its tile. Its arrows are shorter: 3.8 px a point against board 1’s 6.2, so 12 states’ small shifts draw as an arrowhead alone, against six on board 1. The figure in every tile is unchanged. On a phone both draw gray steps, as board 1 approved; at the 326 px drawing a 390 px phone gets, a note names WA, WV and WY, whose tiles are too small for a code.
Why
Board 1’s arrows need tiles 72 px wide, which only a drawing 930 px wide or more gives, and chapter 14 never gives a drawing that width. The round 3 reviewers found S12 drawing gray steps at every desk width, with no arrows, though its entry, reading guide and alt describe arrows.

My first draft kept the 1,024 px frame, because I believed the stacked tile needed a wider column than it does. The cartographer’s measure changed my view. My ruling on this map in the last round put the stacked tile first and a scrolling frame only where it does not fit, and in either drawing the figure in each tile still carries every state’s value.

The data lead’s view.

I agree with the stacked tile. At a 1,440 px window it shows the whole map in the column, every code, figure and arrow, with the chapter list in place; the scrolling frame hides Maine and Rhode Island and the list. Shorter arrows cost little, since every tile prints its figure. The cartographer’s 618 px replaces my 723.

Rule 14.104 and S73

S73, the joint fundraising committees

S73 now draws every committee the Federal Election Commission designates a joint fundraising committee that paid either party’s 2024 presidential campaign: three on the Democratic side and four on the Republican side, in place of one each.

Recommended Approve S73 as drawn.

What changed
The plan picked the one committee per nominee that sent the campaign the most. The chart now reads all seven by that rule, from a new file, with transfers to other committees (line 22) as the measure for both. The Democratic campaign and its main fund carried Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s name until July 21, 2024, so the line under that bar names both candidates with the date, and a note splits that side’s transfers before and after the date. The Republican side kept one candidate and is not split; its two renames are named with their dates.
Why
Read from the right, picking one committee per side drew a contrast in reach, 53 committees against two, that came from the rule that picked them. Read across all seven, both sides reached a similar number of committees: the Democratic funds 54 and the Republican funds 56.
The plan said
One joint fundraising committee per nominee, the one that transferred the most to the nominee’s principal campaign committee.
As built
A new file of all seven committees the FEC designates joint fundraising committees of the two campaigns, with transfers on line 22 and refunds on line 28C set apart.

Rule 14.110 and S76

S76, where 2024 House campaign money came from and went

S76 now nets the transfers between each campaign and its own other committees candidate by candidate, and draws the money sent out as its own band.

Recommended Approve S76 as drawn.

What changed
The file had netted transfers across all 1,926 campaigns at once, which left $156.8 million in and nothing out. Netted for each candidate, $175.1 million came in and $18.3 million went out. The money left unaccounted for stays $1.5 million, and a note says 297 campaigns’ figures do not balance, with one campaign leaving nearly all of it.
Why
Netting across campaigns cancels one campaign’s money out against another’s money in, and those dollars never met. The note promised candidate-by-candidate netting.
The plan said
Transfers between a candidate’s own committees are netted out.
As built
The same file, with transfers netted candidate by candidate.

Medicaid renewals: the atlas’s 25 million against CMS’s own count

The atlas says more than 25 million people were disenrolled when pandemic-era Medicaid rules ended, 69 percent for a procedural reason. Its claims give KFF’s count to September 12, 2024, but Issue I062 “Paperwork pushes eligible people off benefits”, Issue I133 “Coverage gaps and renewal paperwork interrupt health care” and three pathways print the figure with no period. CMS’s own file, which S65 draws, counts 22,914,537 renewals ended for renewals due April 2023 to March 2024, 69.7 percent for a procedural reason.

Recommended In V7.1, print KFF’s period beside the 25 million wherever the atlas gives the figure without one, and keep the figure. The guide keeps printing CMS’s figures with CMS’s period on S65 and corrects nothing in the atlas.

What changed
Nothing in the guide. The two counts come from different publishers, months and counting rules, so neither shows the other wrong.
Why
A figure without its period cannot be checked against another count.

Reform R-01’s two ballot measures, decided after the snapshot

The atlas’s snapshot of October 15, 2026 describes Alaska’s Ballot Measure 2 and Massachusetts Question 3 as pending; 49 text fields name one or both. Both were decided on November 3. Alaska’s unofficial count of November 12 has Measure 2 at 47.19 percent yes and 52.81 percent no, with every precinct in. Question 3 lost, 38.96 percent yes to 61.04 percent no, by NBC Boston’s unofficial results with the Associated Press’s call, a secondary source read November 11. Neither state has certified.

Recommended In V7.1, rewrite the places that name either measure from each state’s certified result, with its date, once both certify; Alaska aims for November 25, 2026. The guide prints the outcomes in one place, the first note of S03 and S08, dated November 11, 2026, with Alaska’s unofficial count of November 10, 47.4 percent yes to 52.6 no. Those notes keep that count until all three measures they name are certified, then change once. The November 12 count above is a later unofficial read, shown on this board only.

What changed
Nothing in the guide.
Why
The records were right on October 15, 2026 and are out of date now.

The atlas’s wording of the Article V route

The atlas’s route for a constitutional amendment reads “Two-thirds of each house of Congress and three-quarters of the states, or a convention”, with no source. Article V gives two ways to propose an amendment, by two-thirds of both houses or by a convention the states call, and two ways to ratify it, by three-quarters of the states’ legislatures or of state conventions.

Recommended In V7.1, rewrite the route to name both ways to propose and both ways to ratify, citing Article V.

What changed
Nothing in the guide: S37’s note prints the studio’s own sentence.
Why
Read as written, a convention could seem to amend the Constitution alone; under Article V a convention only proposes, and three-quarters of the states must still ratify.
V7.1 list
New to the list

Nothing in the guide, which names the bill with both provisions at first mention in each chapter.
Why
“A ban” alone leaves out the bill’s second provision, which a reader who backs photo ID laws and a reader who opposes them both need to know the bill holds.
V7.1 list
Partly new: item 36 covers the bill’s status entry, not these two places

Issue titles that state an effect

Three issue titles S63 prints state an effect: “Withholding appropriated money weakens Congress’s spending decisions”, “Firing and emptying watchdog offices weakens oversight” and “At-will removal of regulators narrows agency independence”. A reread of the atlas’s 334 headings for six such verbs (weaken, narrow, threaten, drain, dilute, harm) finds them in 16 issue titles and 2 loop titles across several domains; five of the titles concern a president’s or the executive’s actions.

Recommended In V7.1, read all 18 titles by one test: a title states an effect only as firmly as the issue’s own grade for that effect allows, and otherwise names the action the record documents.

What changed
Nothing in the guide, which prints atlas titles as stored with their grade beside them.
Why
A title that states an effect reads as the atlas’s verdict, and the same test has to reach every title, whoever the actor is.
V7.1 list
New to the list

One name for each variable: the loop label or the variable’s title Reply 5 You decide

The atlas gives 24 of the 25 variables in its numbered loops two names: a title on the variable and a shorter label inside each loop. Several loop labels carry a verdict or a term a reader has to look up: “Executive unilateralism” for presidential action without new legislation, “Policy tilt to insiders” for policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests, “Affective polarization” for hostility toward the other political party. The guide prints the loop labels inside loops and the titles elsewhere, and chapters 10 and 11 use “Executive unilateralism” as the name of Civic Line icon CL-026.

Should every variable’s own title replace its loop label wherever the guide draws a loop, in chapters 10, 11 and 15 together?

Recommended Yes. Use each variable’s title in every loop drawing in chapters 10, 11 and 15, and ask V7.1 to do the same, so each variable has one name. The titles run longer, 36.5 characters on average against 22.0, so loop drawings need more room, and Civic Line icon CL-026 would print “Presidential action without new legislation” in place of “Executive unilateralism”.

What changed
Nothing yet. Until you answer, chapter 15 keeps loop labels inside loops and the titles of variables D1, D2, D4 and D6 outside them.
Why
Two names for one variable make a reader ask whether they are two things, and the titles are the plainer names, with no verdict in them.

Rule 14.45 · Avoid · Round 1 · Maker B

Open the live entry

Streamgraph Form to avoid

Avoid streamgraphs, whose layers float on a baseline no one can read.

Use it when No reader’s question calls for it. A reader who asks how the parts of a total changed over time gets a truer answer from small multiples or a stacked area.

Timeline

Reader question Which rule changes since 1870 decided who counts, who governs, who owns and who checks?

Finding

The atlas traces 24 rule changes since 1870 on four threads: who counts, who governs, who owns and who checks.

A board 1 chart, changed since board 1. See what changed in panel 1.

On Newsprint

On a narrow screen this frame opens on the phone drawing; scroll it sideways for the 1440 px drawing.

On Charcoal

On a narrow screen this frame opens on the phone drawing; scroll it sideways for the 1440 px drawing.

Grayscale proof of both grounds

Source: Oath & Action’s systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, history, 24 events, February 3, 1870 to June 29, 2026, United States. Snapshot of October 15, 2026. Each event rests on a statute, ruling, constitutional text or official record, cited in its own row; the size of any effect comes from the source named beside it.

13,801 bytes on the page: 13,027 for the chart as the build places it and 774 for the frame round it. Passes every check in the kit.

The table, as the guide prints it: Rule changes since 1870, 24 in all
Rule changes since 1870, 24 in all
DateThreadChangeWhat it did
February 3, 1870Who countsFifteenth Amendment ratifiedBarred race as a voting qualification and left enforcement to Congress and the courts.
November 1, 1890Who countsMississippi adopts its 1890 constitutionLiteracy tests, poll taxes and understanding clauses (which let registrars judge whether an applicant could explain the constitution) spread across the South, and Black registration collapsed within a decade.
April 8, 1913Who governsSeventeenth Amendment ratifiedSenators became directly elected; each state kept two senators regardless of population.
August 18, 1920Who countsNineteenth Amendment ratifiedBarred sex as a voting qualification; the eligible electorate roughly doubled on paper.
June 18, 1929Who governsReapportionment Act of 1929 fixes the House at 435Average district size grew from about 210,000 to about 760,000 people, which reduced constituents’ access to their member and how closely seats track population.
July 5, 1935Who ownsWagner Act (and the Social Security Act, August 14, 1935)Created collective bargaining rights and social insurance, with agricultural and domestic workers excluded.
June 23, 1947Who ownsTaft-Hartley Act passed over a vetoAllowed state right-to-work laws and barred secondary boycotts; union growth stopped in the South.
June 15, 1964Who governsReynolds v. Sims (with Baker v. Carr, 1962, and Wesberry v. Sanders, 1964)Established one person, one vote for state legislatures and House districts, ending the overrepresentation of rural areas.
August 6, 1965Who countsVoting Rights Act signedRequired federal approval (preclearance) of voting changes in covered places and sent federal examiners; Black registration in the South rose from about 30% to over 60% by 1970.
July 10, 1972Who governsMcGovern-Fraser rules take effectBinding primaries and caucuses replaced bargaining at party conventions, so primary voters became the people who choose nominees.
July 12, 1974Who checksCongressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act (Federal Election Campaign Act amendments, October 15, 1974)Made it unlawful for the President to withhold appropriated money without a rescission approved by Congress; the campaign-finance amendments set contribution limits and created the Federal Election Commission.
January 30, 1976Who checksBuckley v. ValeoStruck down spending limits and kept contribution limits; treating campaign money as speech has framed the law for fifty years.
June 6, 1978Who ownsProposition 13 (labor-law reform filibustered June 22, 1978; First National Bank of Boston v. Bellotti, April 26, 1978)The California tax revolt, the defeat of labor-law reform in the Senate and new corporate speech rights arrived in one season.
October 12, 1978Who checksInspector General Act (Ethics in Government Act, October 26, 1978)Created statutory watchdogs inside agencies and required financial disclosure by officials.
January 4, 1995Who governsThe 104th Congress opensThe House cut committee staff by about 41% (2,147 in 1993 to 1,266 in 1995), Congress closed the Office of Technology Assessment and party leaders took more control; expectations that committee members raise money followed.
November 12, 1999Who ownsGramm-Leach-Bliley Act (Commodity Futures Modernization Act, December 21, 2000)Allowed banks, securities firms and insurers to combine, and the 2000 law left most derivatives unregulated; the 2008 crisis and the TARP bank rescue followed.
January 21, 2010Who checksCitizens United v. FEC (SpeechNow.org v. FEC, March 26, 2010)Independent spending by corporations and unions became unlimited; super PACs followed within two months.
June 25, 2013Who countsShelby County v. HolderStruck down the formula that decided which places needed preclearance, which ended preclearance in practice; Texas moved to enforce its voter-ID law the same day.
November 21, 2013Who governsNuclear option for lower-court and executive nominations (extended to the Supreme Court on April 6, 2017)A rules change by simple majority ended the 60-vote threshold for these confirmations, so appointments track which party controls the Senate.
December 22, 2017Who ownsTax Cuts and Jobs ActCut the corporate rate to 21% and made the individual cuts temporary; the resulting deficits fed later arguments for spending cuts.
December 29, 2022Who checksElectoral Count Reform ActMade the Vice President’s role in the count ministerial, required one-fifth of each chamber to raise an objection, made governors’ certificates conclusive and sped up court review.
July 4, 2025Who owns2025 budget reconciliation law, P.L. 119-21 (counter-event: the American Rescue Plan, March 11, 2021)The 2025 law extends the 2017 tax cuts and, by Congressional Budget Office estimates tallied by KFF, cuts federal Medicaid spending by about $1 trillion over 2025 to 2034, with further cuts to SNAP food aid. The 2021 law expanded the child tax credit for one year, when child poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure fell to 5.2%; the expansion then expired.
April 29, 2026Who countsLouisiana v. CallaisThe Supreme Court (6 to 3) held that Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is violated only when the evidence supports a strong inference of intentional discrimination. Within five weeks Florida, Tennessee and Louisiana enacted new congressional maps and the Court let Alabama return to its 2023 plan; each change removed a majority-Black or Black-opportunity district.
June 29, 2026Who checksTrump v. Slaughter and Trump v. Cook (NRSC v. FEC, June 30, 2026; inspector general removals, January 24, 2025; Storch v. Hegseth ruling, September 24, 2025)Trump v. Slaughter overruled Humphrey’s Executor and lets the President remove Federal Trade Commission members at will (6 to 3). The same day, in Trump v. Cook, the Court (5 to 4) declined to let the President remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook while her case continues, an interim order. On June 30, 2026, NRSC v. FEC struck down limits on party committees’ coordinated spending. At least 17 inspectors general were removed on January 24, 2025 without the required notice; on September 24, 2025 a district court said the removals almost undoubtedly violated the notice rule and ordered no reinstatement.

Status of six issues on checks on power, as of October 15, 2026
IssueTitleAtlas gradeStatus, in the atlas’s wordsAtlas checkChecked
Issue I163At-will removal of regulators narrows agency independenceDocumentedOn June 29, 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in Trump v. Slaughter that the President may remove Federal Trade Commission members at will, and it overruled Humphrey’s Executor (1935). The same day, in Trump v. Cook, the Court voted 5 to 4 to deny the government’s request to let the President remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook while her case continues. Cook is an interim order: she stays in office for now, and the Court has not decided whether the Fed’s for-cause protection is valid.updatedOctober 15, 2026
Issue X06An attempted removal tests Federal Reserve independenceDocumentedAs of October 15, 2026, the dispute over removing Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook has been decided only at the stay stage: on June 29, 2026 the Supreme Court, 5 to 4, denied the government’s request to let her removal take effect while the case continues. Congress has not written cause, notice and a hearing for Fed governors into law.partly confirmedOctober 15, 2026
Issue X05Domestic troop deployments test the limits on military powerDocumentedOn December 23, 2025, in Trump v. Illinois, the Supreme Court refused on its emergency docket to lift a lower-court order blocking the deployment of federalized National Guard troops in Illinois. The majority read ‘regular forces’ in the federal statute (10 U.S.C. 12406) as likely meaning the regular U.S. military, so the President would first need legal authority to execute the laws with the military and be unable to do so; the government had not identified that authority. Justices Alito, Thomas and Gorsuch dissented. The order is preliminary.confirmedOctober 15, 2026
Issue I070Firing and emptying watchdog offices weakens oversightDocumentedOn January 24, 2025 at least 17 inspectors general were removed by email without the 30 days’ notice to Congress that the Inspector General Act requires. Eight of them sued (Storch v. Hegseth, U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia). On September 24, 2025 the court said the President almost undoubtedly violated the Act, but it denied reinstatement, because the President could remove them again after giving notice, and it paused the case until the Supreme Court decided Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026). In July 2026 the court set a process for summary-judgment motions, with a conference planned for the week of August 24, 2026. The latest docket entry listed, a July 20, 2026 minute order, shows no ruling on the merits.partly confirmedOctober 15, 2026
Issue I068Withholding appropriated money weakens Congress’s spending decisionsDocumentedThe Impoundment Control Act of 1974 remains in force. The Government Accountability Office, which audits for Congress, found violations in several 2025 decisions, including withheld NIH grant funds (August 5, 2025) and FEMA assistance funds (September 29, 2025), and found two more on October 7, 2026, involving EPA’s Community Change Grants and grants from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. On September 26, 2025 the Supreme Court, acting on an emergency application, let about $4 billion in foreign aid expire after the President proposed rescinding it so late in the fiscal year that the money lapsed before Congress acted, a move called a pocket rescission. The Court’s preliminary view was that the Act likely bars grant recipients from suing under the Administrative Procedure Act to enforce the appropriation.updatedOctober 15, 2026
Issue X18Where a case is filed can decide which judge hears itDocumentedThe Congressional Research Service (report R49022, July 7, 2026) counted 34 cases in which federal courts issued nationwide injunctions against the second Trump administration between January 20, 2025 and June 27, 2025, the day the Supreme Court decided Trump v. CASA, and 16 more cases from June 28, 2025 to June 27, 2026, for 50 in all.confirmedOctober 15, 2026

Panel 3

Rules 14.1 to 14.14 and the opener

These are the fourteen rules every chart follows, as rounds 1 to 3 left them. Each shows its title with its correct and failure plates, photographed from today’s build at a 1440 px window.

The chapter’s opening plate

Rule 14.1 Open the live entry Start from the reader’s question, then choose the form.

Rule 14.2 Open the live entry Build every chart in one anatomy, from evidence label to table.

Rule 14.3 Open the live entry Label the data directly, and use a key only when labels cannot fit.

Rule 14.4 Open the live entry Start bars and columns at zero, keep one scale per axis, and size circles by area.

Rule 14.5 Open the live entry Give each color in a chart one job from the four data palettes.

Rule 14.6 Open the live entry Spend the view’s one red on the point the title names.

Rule 14.7 Open the live entry Tell parties apart by name, place and shape, with no red and blue.

Rule 14.8 Open the live entry Past four groups, split into small multiples or set one group in ink against gray.

Rule 14.9 Open the live entry Show the publisher’s uncertainty, and rank only where a gap passes the margin of error.

Rule 14.10 Open the live entry Choose the window from the question, and draw an inauguration only as a dated note.

Rule 14.11 Open the live entry Mark a gap, a break in a series or a preliminary value in the drawing.

Rule 14.12 Open the live entry Redraw for a phone only when the form must change, and keep the data and finding.

Rule 14.13 Open the live entry Carry every chart’s table as live text, and publish the still image first.

Rule 14.14 Open the live entry Export every chart from the kit, so its files match the page.
